newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK could need 3,000 hectares of land up to 2011.
newsitem.headline: HK could need 3,000 hectares of land up to 2011.

text.p: Hong Kong could need as much as 3,000 hectares of land for urban uses and port activities up to 2011, the government said on Thursday.

"We estimate that up to 2011 Hong Kong could need as much as about 1,500 hectares of land for urban uses and a further equivalent amount for port activities," Secretary for Planning, Environment and Lands, Bowen Leung, said in a statement.
"Population growth coupled with greater affluence and rising expectations create demand for land," he said.
The population of Hong Kong would rise from its current level of 6.3 million to 7.8 million by 2011, and to 8.2 million by 2016, he said.

"Substantial needs for land also arise from the growing and changing hub functions of Hong Kong as a high capacity container port, an international focal point for aviation, and a global and regional centre for business and finance," Leung said.

"Further demand for land arises from the need to support Hong Kong's functions as a centre for high-value-added, commercially-based services, as a base for more high-value-added and high-technology industries, and as a multi-functional headquarters that provides support services for industrial development in South China," he said.
The redevelopment and restructuring of such inner city areas, which had become obsolete, also called for the provision of new areas of land in nearby locations, Leung said.
"Provision of necessary infrastructure to support population and economic growth also requires additional land," he said.

New developable land supply in the territory, with a total land area of less than 1,100 square kilometres, could come from the redevelopment of obsolete and derelict areas, from lowland areas previously used for rural activities, and from reclamation from the sea, he said.
"Such potential sources are expected to provide new strategic growth areas to satisfy our medium and long-term land requirements," he said.

To meet imminent development needs, particularly housing land to keep in pace with the population growth, the authorities had explored alternatives to ensure adequate supply of land and infrastructure by 2006, Leung said.

Those included measures to accelerate existing plans and programmes, to streamline existing mechanisms and to initiate steps to facilitate the development process for both the public and private sectors, he said.
The government was studying the feasibility of new housing sites and trying to expand strategic growth areas, Leung said.

It was also looking into ways to expedite the restructuring of existing obsolete industrial areas in inner city areas for redevelopment into commercial and residential and other suitable uses, Leung said.

The government was considering rezoning surplus industrial land at suitable locations subject to infrastructure capacity, and examining ways to enhance residential development by speeding up urban renewal.

It would also seek to encourage private sector to join in land development by considering measures to speed up the planning process, land transactions and building plan examination, and to resolve environmental constraints, he said.
